en: Others spoke and said,
"While crossing, the young man will tumble,
And his head will be torn off."
Some maidens said,
"He will cross the Urgench and come;
His horse is formidable."
Then Churok said:
"Do not howl, poor women!
Whether he will cross and die,
God alone knows."
Kulchoro saw the maidens;
The poor champion, captivated by their beauty,
With the red horse Buurul,
Turning the ill-fated gray horse at an angle,
He saw the maidens and grew excited;
Without looking all around,
Without sparing his life before that sea,
Without searching all about.
The doomed man who had seen the maidens,
Before the formidable Urgench he had entered,
Did not value his life by so much as a hair:
"Damn this childishness!
If I fear flowing water,
May God strike me outright!
Does the bare-fanged Azrael
Stand watching for me,
Thinking, 'Kulchoro will cross the river'?
If I truly fear the rushing water,
May God strike me outright!
I fear the rushing water;
Yet if a challenge arose in a place of torment,
Brandishing their spears and shouting,
If six thousand enemies came forth,
How could I not fear them?
My elder brother Semetey
Gave me his horse without begrudging it;
Ignoring the horse's own desire,
Saying, 'The flowing water is fierce,'
How can I disgrace myself and turn away?
He gave me his coat without begrudging it;
Ignoring the coat's own worth,
Before I have even seen hell,
Saying, 'The speechless water is evil,'
How can I disgrace myself and turn away?
Rather than hear reproach from my elder brother,
Let me die in the rushing water;
Whatever Allah has written for me,
Let me bear it upon my neck and see!
If the flowing water brings my death,
Let me die this very moment!"
Without searching around for a ford,
The formidable, extraordinary Kulchoro,
Not valuing his life by so much as a hair, said:
"If I should perish upon the road,
I trust in you—Allah, uphold me!
If I live, grant me what has been gathered;
If I die, grant me faith!
Rather than be mocked by the maidens,
Let me behold the face of Judgment Day;
Rather than be mocked by women,
Let me be swept away and die in this water,
And behold the world beyond this passing life!"
Mounted on Buurul, he entered the Urgench,
Shouting, "Almambet!"
And raising the battle cry, "Manas!"
He swung the black-jawed whip,
Gripping it in his hand;
He drew the spirit-like Buurul
Sideways and let him go.
As the maidens stood crowding the bank,
He broke away the top of the bluff,
Prayed to the Creator,
And Kulchoro plunged into the water at a gallop.
The top of the bluff broke apart,
And a mass of earth as large as a house collapsed,
Pouring into the water with him.
The truly spirit-like horse Buurul
Stumbled where he entered,
Recovered from the stumble,
Braced himself and gathered his strength,
Then vanished beneath the water where he entered.
When your Buurul disappeared,
Thirty brides and thirty maidens
Crowded around and wailed;
They clapped their palms together,
Crying out as though a husband had died.
Many maidens, seeking to help,
Ran up and down;
They despaired of Kulchoro,
And the maidens, distraught, cried out,
Wailing as though a husband had died.
"If only that dear young man would come,
So we might see him to our hearts' desire;
If only we could embrace the young man once,
And then afterward die," they say—
Thus your maidens go about wishing.
"There are many souls among our people,
And many boys of twelve;
They cannot manage to put on their clothes,
Nor cover their hems when they urinate.
Even now those boys
Feel no shame before their mothers.
The red flower has faded," they say;
"The tender young sapling
Has journeyed toward Judgment Day," they say.
The maidens, distraught, wailed,
Crying out as though a husband had died.
His white steel gathering rust,
The practiced horse Buurul
Would not yield to the Urgench,
But strained toward the heart of its current.
His blue steel gathering rust,
Having crossed many lakes and rivers,
The seasoned horse Buurul
Strained toward the place where the waters converged.
His front teeth flashed;
Without veering up or down,
The practiced horse Buurul
Swam straight across through the roar.
Over the champion, noble as a prince,
White foam streamed visibly;
That white foam thundered,
Surged over the young man's head,
And poured down.
When they saw that foam,
The many maidens watching cried,
"Now he truly is dead,"
And tears poured from their eyes.
Kulchoro, upheld by holy spirits,
Upon the red horse Buurul,
Came on with growing force before their eyes.
As he gained strength, the maidens rejoiced
And wailed, crying, "Baabedin!"
Just as he drew near,
Another marvel appeared:
Waves gathered as large as houses,
Colliding with one another,
And rushed down in fury.
When they were about to engulf him,
About to pass over him and bring death,
Your champion, Almambet's son,
Raised his spear;
The wave that came from ahead
He thrust away before him,
And the wave that came from behind
He swept away behind him.
Like one thoroughly skilled,
Thus Kulchoro came onward.
Nine spirits supported him;
It was the moment they held him up.
Nine spirits upheld him;
It was the hour they took him under their protection.
There in the water, the naked Khizr
And young Aydar took the young man
By his horse's reins.
The forty chilten and Khizr Ilyas
Loudly cheered and urged him on.
The giant black bird, the Simurgh,
As though to carry the young man
Away from within the water,
Stretched down its talons
And came swooping upon him.
The splendid horse Buurul
Swam unwaveringly through the Urgench.
I could make myself a sacrifice for that steed!
There is a circling white cliff and a deep pool;
If Arbuudan should drift downstream,
There is a bank where death is certain.
Buurul knows that as well.
Without drifting downstream, he swam straight on;
A creature wiser than a mere beast,
He swam strongly, neither hurrying nor faltering.
A creature wiser than a mere beast,
Akun's daughter Churok—
He took his course straight toward her.
At the place called Bugu-Kechuu,
Your steed did not turn aside
But drew close to the bank.
He curved his neck like a stag,
And without delay sprang from that bank,
Leaping up onto the high ground.
He emerged from the water, sleek and gleaming;
From the corners of the leather saddle cloth
And the blue felt pad, water squelched.
Ah, that creature, the horse Buurul,
Stepped forward and began to amble;
From the corners of the broad saddle cloth
Water poured and streamed.
Sleek as a hunting hound,
With golden shoes and silver nails,
The true courser Buurul's hooves
Flashed beneath him.
His wet hair lay divided into channels;
The water flowing from mane and tail
Fell away in separate streams.
Each vertebra and rib,
Each separate bone, stood visible.
The splendid, well-fleshed creature,
Whose calf was as thick as a bull's waist,
Whose stride was like the wind of the steppe,
When he drew near the maidens,
Moved sleekly at an amble,
Showing off his spirited ways.
The creature assumed every kind of bearing,
Tossing his forelock toward the sky,
Driving his hooves against the earth;
The black-steel bit
Rattled against his throat.
His tail, like willow silk,
Lashed against his spreading thighs.
Every strand of hair stood apart,
And to the people watching,
The marks of a true courser showed plainly.
Those who watched him thought,
"If only that were my horse";
Whoever saw him burned with longing.
Ah, that creature, the horse Buurul—
If you saw his forelock, so beautiful,
You would measure it against your eye and knot it there.
The rider mounted upon him
Was Kulchoro, upheld by holy spirits.
If seven hundred thousand black-clad troops came,
He could plunge among them alone.
If an enemy came with spear made ready,
His calf was as thick as a bull's waist,
His stride was like the wind of the steppe.

The rider mounted upon him
Was Kulchoro, upheld by holy spirits.
If seven hundred thousand black-clad troops came,

If an enemy came with spear made ready,
He could enter and range among them alone;
Before anyone could utter a word,
He seemed able to strike the whole world.
The gold-edged battle-axe
Seemed ready now to enter the foe,
Hanging at his wrist.
